query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In single‐phase high-entropy alloys, mechanical loading under service conditions drives a localized atomic reordering (or nanophase separation) at the grain boundaries that produces subtle nanoscale compositional fluctuations, thereby reducing intergranular cohesion and promoting brittle failure.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, single-phase, compositionally complex high-entropy alloy (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi) with uniformly distributed elements and pristine, unmodified grain boundaries.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled series of deformation experiments in which strain rate and thermal exposure are systematically varied. Specimens with a pre-strain thermal history designed to pre-activate or modify the grain boundary state are compared to controls with pristine thermal histories. In situ TEM and atom-probe tomography are used to monitor grain boundary structure during and after deformation.
generation.conditions: Service-relevant temperatures encompassing regimes for both high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement, with controlled strain rates and under ultra-high vacuum to prevent extrinsic impurity segregation.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries undergoing stress-induced local atomic reordering (nanophase separation) that creates nanoscale compositional fluctuations.
generation.mechanism: Under applied loading, the stress drives a reordering of atoms at the grain boundaries even in a chemically uniform alloy. This localized rearrangement leads to nanometer-scale heterogeneities that weaken the cohesion between grains, facilitating intergranular brittle fracture without the traditional roles of segregation or precipitate formation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Specimens with pre-activated (thermally modified) grain boundaries will, under critical strain rate and temperature conditions, exhibit detectable local atomic reordering (via in situ TEM and atom-probe tomography) alongside reduced fracture strains and observable intergranular decohesion. In contrast, pristine specimens should retain uniform grain boundary structure and higher ductility.
generation.baseline: Pristine HEA specimens with thermally unaltered, uniform grain boundaries showing high toughness and ductility under similar loading conditions.
generation.boundary: The mechanism is expected to be active only under service conditions where a sufficient combination of thermal activation and strain rate exists to drive the stress-induced reordering. At temperatures or strain rates too low to induce atomic reordering, the alloy should behave in a conventionally ductile manner.
generation.uncertainty: The exact kinetics and magnitude of the stress-induced atomic reordering, as well as the precise threshold strain rate and temperature necessary to trigger this process, remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA specimens: one set undergoes a pre-strain thermal treatment designed to promote early onset of grain boundary atomic reordering while the control set remains with pristine grain boundaries. Both sets are then subjected to identical deformation protocols at service-relevant temperatures and strain rates in ultra-high vacuum. Grain boundary evolution is monitored in real time using in situ TEM, and post-deformation analyses are conducted using atom-probe tomography.
measurements: Grain boundary atomic structure and presence of nanoscale compositional fluctuations (via in situ TEM and atom-probe tomography)
Tensile fracture strain and ductility metrics
Fractographic analysis to determine if failure is predominantly intergranular
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-treated and pristine specimens exhibit identical grain boundary structures (i.e., no observable stress-induced atomic reordering or nanophase separation) and similar ductility and failure modes under the same conditions, the hypothesis that stress-induced grain boundary reordering is responsible for emergent brittleness is falsified.

The effect of serrated grain boundary on tensile and creep properties has been investigated for a high-entropy alloy (Al8Co35Cr18Ni34Ti3Nb2Zr0.005B0.01 (at.%)) fabricated by selective laser melting, the followings are findings of this work: Serrated grain boundary could render a significant increase in tensile fracture strain and creep rupture life by a factor of 3.5 and 400, respectively. The inferior ductility of straight grain boundary at 650°C was attributed to the grain boundary embrittlement caused by strain concentration at triple junctions and fast intergranular crack propagation. The slow cooling process of the post heat treatment could coarsen the γ′ particles and encourage interactions with mobile grain boundaries to from serrated grain boundaries. Analysis has indicated that serrated grain boundary could distribute strains more evenly than that of straight morphology. Serrated grain boundaries could reduce local strain concentration and provide resistance against intergranular cracking.

decision.trend: Early studies on high‐entropy alloys focused on the remarkable resistance of these single‐phase materials to the conventional causes of toughness degradation—namely, grain‐boundary segregation and brittle intermetallic precipitation. As research progressed, groups began to demonstrate that fine modifications of the grain-boundary morphology (e.g., inducing a serrated rather than straight boundary) can substantially improve ductility and delay intergranular fracture. In effect, while conventional alloys lose toughness through extrinsically driven chemical inhomogeneities at grain boundaries, the trend in HEAs has moved toward an investigation of intrinsic, stress‐induced, microstructural evolutions at the boundaries (or near-boundary regions) that may later lead to brittle behavior. Yet, even with promising work on controlled boundary morphology, the causative link between stress-induced local reordering at a chemically uniform grain boundary and emergent brittleness in an initially single‐phase HEA remains to be established.
decision.unsolved: The open question is whether, in the absence of conventional segregation or precipitate formation, the onset of brittle behavior is instead governed by an intrinsic stress-driven reordering (or nanophase separation) at the grain boundaries. This mechanism would be distinct from classical models and remains untested under service-like strain and temperature regimes.
decision.lever: Perform a systematic series of deformation experiments in which strain rate and thermal exposure are carefully varied to induce—and then in situ monitor—the onset of stress-driven atomic reordering at grain boundaries, using advanced characterization tools like in situ TEM and atom-probe tomography. The experiment would compare specimens with nearly identical bulk compositions but with different pre-strain thermal histories (to subtly influence the 'state' of the grain boundaries) under controlled loading.
decision.why: This approach directly tests the hypothesis that intrinsic grain-boundary reordering, rather than conventional segregation or precipitate formation, is responsible for toughness degradation in single-phase HEAs. It follows naturally from the observed benefits of boundary serration in previous studies, thereby isolating a variable (local atomic ordering at the GBs) that conventional alloys do not exhibit under similar conditions.
